claims.claim: Stonehenge's Altar Stone was traced to Scotland in 2024. Where exactly it came from is still unknown
claims.source_checked: api.crossref.org/works/10.1038/s41586-024-07652-1 (title, abstract, online 2024-08-14); Clarke 2024 full text via pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov OAI-PMH JATS record (oai:pubmedcentral.nih.gov:11324516) and research index pmcid:PMC11324516; api.crossref.org/works/10.1144/jgs2026-090 (ABSTRACT ONLY); api.crossref.org/works/10.1002/jqs.70080 (ABSTRACT ONLY)
claims.note: Clarke 2024 title 'A Scottish provenance for the Altar Stone of Stonehenge' (online 14 Aug 2024); body: isotopic data 'indicate that the Altar Stone of Stonehenge has a provenance from the ORS in the Orcadian Basin of northeast Scotland'. Pirrie 2026 abstract: 'the exact provenance of the Altar Stone is as yet unknown'; Clarke 2026 abstract: 'its source location within this large basin remains unresolved'. Neither abstract says the stone is not Scottish (Pirrie: grain dating 'supports a Laurentian source'). Caveat: both 2026 papers read as abstracts only.

claims.claim: In 2024, Stonehenge's Altar Stone was traced to Scotland.
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1038/s41586-024-07652-1: Crossref abstract; full text (PMC OAI JATS record; research index pmcid:PMC11324516)
claims.note: A4: a viewer who swipes at second two takes away 'a 2024 study traced it to Scotland', which is what the paper did (abstract: 'remarkable similarity to the Old Red Sandstone of the Orcadian Basin in northeast Scotland'). Clarke 2024 notes Svalbard ORS is also statistically indistinguishable in zircon ages but still concludes NE Scotland; the 2026 abstracts narrow the source within the basin but do not reject Scotland. 'Traced' is a fair reading of the paper's own claim.

claims.claim: Exactly where it came from is still unknown.

claims.note: Pirrie 2026 abstract: 'the exact provenance of the Altar Stone is as yet unknown'. Clarke 2026 abstract: 'its source location within this large basin remains unresolved'. 'Still' holds: Parker Pearson 2024: 'As yet, the actual outcrop from which the Altar Stone was extracted is unknown'.

claims.claim: 'Stonehenge (approx.)' pin at 51.179 N, 1.826 W
claims.source_checked: Clarke 2024 Fig. 4a image (cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/cb4e/11324516/19b0b3f0291b/41586_2024_7652_Fig4_HTML.jpg); historicengland.org.uk, whc.unesco.org, wikidata, OS and geonames hosts refused (403/blocked); Marine Regions has no record
claims.note: Confirmed only at the precision the label claims. claims.claim: The ages of tiny mineral grains inside it matched sandstone in the northeast.
claims.source_checked: Clarke 2024 full text (PMC OAI JATS; research index pmcid:PMC11324516) and Crossref abstract
claims.note: Clarke 2024 dates zircon, apatite and rutile from Altar Stone thin sections, with grains 'typically 10-40 um wide' (so 'tiny' holds). 'The detrital zircon age spectra from Orcadian Basin ORS provides the closest match to the Altar Stone detrital ages' (KS test P > 0.05). 'Apatite U-Pb age components from Orcadian Basin samples from Spittal, Caithness (AQ1) and Cruaday, Orkney (CQ1) ... match those from the Altar Stone.' 'The northeast' follows 'Scotland' in the hook.

claims.note: Every vertex is at sea, no segment crosses a coast ring, and no sampled point lies on land. claims.claim: A glacier? A 2026 ice model says ice could have carried it part of the way, at most.
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1002/jqs.70080 ABSTRACT ONLY (api.crossref.org; Wiley full text 403 bot challenge; not in research index); Crossref published-online 2026-06-04
claims.note: Abstract: 'we combine sandstone provenance analysis with ice flow modelling'; 'Glacial dispersal to Dogger Bank would reduce the anthropogenic transport distance required to Stonehenge from 700 km to 400 km'; 'Glacial transport may have provided an intermediate stage in the stone's journey, but alone cannot account for the final emplacement on Salisbury Plain.' 'Could have ... part of the way, at most' matches 'may have provided an intermediate stage ... alone cannot account'. The script leaves out the abstract's further 'temporal problem' (Dogger Bank inundated before the stone likely arrived), which only weakens the ice idea, so the line does not overstate. Confirmed from the abstract only.

claims.claim: Six tonnes, from a spot no one has pinned down, by a route no one knows.
claims.source_checked: Clarke 2024 abstract and full text; Parker Pearson 2024 full text; Clarke 2026 and Pirrie 2026 ABSTRACTS ONLY
claims.note: Recap. Six tonnes: claim 13. Spot unknown: claim 3. Route unknown: Clarke 2024 suggests sea but names no route; Parker Pearson 2024 says transport 'can only have been achieved in two ways - by land or by water (or a combination of both)' and says only that 'a land route may have been favoured'; Clarke 2026 leaves the mode 'uncertain' (abstract: 'its mode of transport uncertain').

claims.claim: Sea, sledge or ice: how do you think it got there?
claims.source_checked: Clarke 2024 abstract; Parker Pearson 2024 full text; Clarke 2026 ABSTRACT ONLY
claims.note: Clarke 2026 lists the 'Proposed mechanisms' as 'marine or overland routes or southward movement as a glacial erratic', so the three options are the ones in the literature. Ice was qualified as 'part of the way, at most' two lines earlier and on screen. E2: the line asks the viewer's opinion. It has no instruction to comment, no 'comment X' prompt, and no promise the short does not keep, so it does not break E2. It is still a soft engagement prompt; the owner may prefer to cut it.
